subtopic_detail: Acute vestibular syndrome and bedside oculomotor testing
stem:
You are the emergency registrar assessing a 58 year old man who has had continuous spinning dizziness for six hours, with vomiting and inability to stand unaided. He has hypertension and smokes 20 cigarettes a day. He reports no headache and no change in his hearing.

On examination he has horizontal nystagmus beating to the right that does not change direction on left or right gaze. The head impulse test produces no corrective saccade when his head is turned to either side. Cover test reveals a vertical shift of the left eye on uncovering. Limb power, coordination and speech are normal. He cannot walk without two people supporting him.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 168/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Non-contrast CT brain reported as no acute intracranial abnormality; blood glucose 6.1 mmol/L (4.0-7.8)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Prescribe prochlorperazine and discharge with written vestibular sedative advice
options.rationale: Vestibular sedatives suppress central compensation and are recommended only for short term symptom relief, and discharge is unsafe when the bedside examination points to a central cause. Prochlorperazine would be reasonable only once a central lesion had been excluded. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer for outpatient audiometry and formal vestibular function testing next week
options.rationale: Deferred testing does not address a patient who cannot mobilise and has central signs, and audiometry is most useful when hearing loss accompanies the vertigo, which he denies. Outpatient pathways are appropriate for recurrent stable dizziness. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Vertigo)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Vertigo

options.text: Perform Dix-Hallpike testing and treat with an Epley repositioning manoeuvre
options.rationale: Repositioning treats benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which causes brief positionally triggered attacks with fatiguing torsional nystagmus, not six hours of continuous vertigo with spontaneous direction-fixed nystagmus. The distinction is episodic and positional versus continuous and spontaneous. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Vertigo)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Vertigo

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone for presumed inflammation of the vestibular nerve
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are used for vestibular neuritis, but that peripheral diagnosis requires an abnormal head impulse test with a corrective saccade and no skew deviation, and the near-pair distinction from a central lesion turns precisely on those two findings. Treating for neuritis here would delay reperfusion assessment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange urgent MRI brain with diffusion weighted imaging and stroke unit admission
options.rationale: A normal head impulse test with skew deviation in a patient with continuous vertigo and severe gait failure indicates a central lesion, and posterior fossa infarction is missed by non-contrast CT in the majority of cases within the first 24 hours. Diffusion weighted MRI is the imaging that changes management here. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management
BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Vertigo

explanation.summary: Acute vestibular syndrome describes continuous vertigo lasting more than 24 hours with nystagmus, nausea and gait disturbance, and the central versus peripheral split drives everything that follows. The three-step bedside oculomotor battery of head impulse, nystagmus and test of skew outperforms early CT for detecting posterior circulation infarction, because thin bone artefact and small infarct volume make CT insensitive in the posterior fossa. A peripheral pattern is an abnormal head impulse test with a corrective saccade, direction-fixed nystagmus and no skew. Any one central feature moves the patient onto a stroke pathway with MRI, admission and vascular risk factor management. Missed cerebellar infarction carries the risk of malignant oedema and brainstem compression over the subsequent 48 to 72 hours.
key_points: Continuous vertigo with severe truncal ataxia raises the probability of a central lesion regardless of a normal CT
A normal head impulse test in a patient with genuine acute vestibular syndrome is a central finding, not a reassuring one
Skew deviation on cover testing is highly specific for a brainstem lesion
Non-contrast CT misses most posterior fossa infarcts in the first 24 hours
Vestibular sedatives should be limited to short courses because they delay central compensation
explanation.pearls: In acute vestibular syndrome the head impulse test reads backwards from intuition: a normal result, meaning no corrective saccade, points to a central lesion and mandates diffusion weighted MRI rather than discharge.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation: Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management
BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Vertigo

subtopic_detail: Acute unilateral facial weakness and corticosteroid timing
stem:
A 34 year old woman presents to your general practice clinic with drooping of the left side of her face that she first noticed on waking 30 hours ago. She describes her eye watering and food collecting in her left cheek, and says sounds seem uncomfortably loud on that side.

On examination she cannot wrinkle her left forehead or bury her left eyelashes, and the left corner of her mouth does not move on smiling. There is no rash in or around the ear and the tympanic membranes are normal. Limb power, sensation and coordination are normal, and her speech is clear. She is not pregnant and has no history of diabetes.

data_table.Examination: Complete left facial weakness including the forehead; Bell phenomenon present; corneal reflex intact; no vesicles in the external auditory canal; no parotid mass

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Provide eye lubrication and review in one week to assess spontaneous recovery
options.rationale: Watchful waiting forfeits the benefit of early corticosteroids, and by the review date the treatment window will have closed. Supportive care alone is what remains available for patients who present after 72 hours. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start oral aciclovir alone, with eye lubrication and overnight eye taping
options.rationale: Antiviral monotherapy does not improve outcomes and is only considered added to a corticosteroid in severe or complete palsy; alone it leaves the intervention with proven benefit unused. Antivirals become the priority when vesicles indicate herpes zoster of the ear rather than this presentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange urgent CT brain before any drug treatment is commenced
options.rationale: Forehead involvement localises the lesion to the lower motor neuron, so imaging is not required in an otherwise normal neurological examination and would push her past the treatment window. Urgent imaging is indicated when the forehead is spared or other cranial nerve or limb signs appear. (Source: RACGP: Bell Palsy Management)

options.text: Arrange serology and defer treatment until the results are available
options.rationale: Waiting for serology would delay corticosteroids beyond the 72 hour window for a condition that is a clinical diagnosis. Targeted serology belongs in patients with tick exposure in an endemic region or bilateral palsy. (Source: RACGP: Bell Palsy Management)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone now, with eye lubrication and overnight eye taping
options.rationale: Corticosteroids started within 72 hours of symptom onset significantly increase the rate of complete recovery, and she is at 30 hours, so treatment should begin at this visit rather than after investigation. Eye protection is mandatory because incomplete lid closure risks exposure keratopathy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Acute idiopathic lower motor neuron facial palsy is diagnosed clinically, and the single decision that most affects outcome is whether a corticosteroid is started inside the first 72 hours. Forehead involvement is the finding that separates a peripheral seventh nerve lesion from a cortical lesion, in which the upper face is preserved by bilateral cortical input. Hyperacusis and altered taste reflect involvement of the nerve to stapedius and the chorda tympani respectively, and locate the lesion within the facial canal. Around 70 per cent of untreated patients recover completely, rising with early corticosteroid treatment. The most common preventable complication is corneal injury from failure of lid closure, so eye care is prescribed alongside the steroid at the first visit.
key_points: Forehead sparing indicates an upper motor neuron lesion and demands urgent imaging instead
Corticosteroid benefit depends on starting within 72 hours of symptom onset
Antivirals are added only in severe or complete palsy, never used alone
Vesicles in the ear canal indicate herpes zoster oticus and change the treatment
Lubricants and overnight taping prevent exposure keratopathy while lid closure is incomplete
explanation.pearls: The therapeutic window is the examinable number: oral prednisolone started within 72 hours of onset improves complete recovery rates, and no investigation should be allowed to push a typical presentation past that mark.

subtopic_detail: Proximal weakness and bone pain with a low calcium and raised alkaline phosphatase
stem:
A 58 year old woman is referred to you with eight months of aching in her hips, thighs and ribs, and increasing difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs without pulling on the handrail. She has fallen twice.

She moved to Australia from Afghanistan 11 years ago, wears concealing clothing outdoors and rarely leaves the house during daylight. She eats very little dairy. She takes no corticosteroids, anticonvulsants or antiretroviral medicines and has had no gastrointestinal surgery. On examination she has symmetrical proximal weakness with a waddling gait, and tenderness when firm pressure is applied over the ribs and pelvis. There is no rash, no synovitis and no scalp tenderness.

data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.06 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), phosphate 0.62 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), alkaline phosphatase 320 U/L (30-110), parathyroid hormone 14.8 pmol/L (1.6-6.9), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 12 nmol/L (sufficient above 50), creatinine 71 micromol/L (45-90), creatine kinase within normal limits, erythrocyte sedimentation rate within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone at 15 mg daily for probable polymyalgia rheumatica
options.rationale: Polymyalgia rheumatica causes girdle pain with stiffness and a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and hers is normal while the biochemistry gives a complete alternative explanation. Corticosteroids would also accelerate the bone loss already present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Commence a weekly oral bisphosphonate with calcium and review her in three months
options.rationale: Giving a bisphosphonate before correcting the deficiency risks precipitating symptomatic hypocalcaemia, because mineral is drawn into unmineralised bone once resorption is blocked. Antiresorptive therapy is considered only after vitamin D and calcium have been replete for some months. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for parathyroidectomy after parathyroid localisation imaging is completed
options.rationale: Her raised parathyroid hormone is an appropriate secondary response to a low calcium, whereas primary hyperparathyroidism raises the calcium. The near-pair distinction rests entirely on whether the calcium is high or low alongside the raised hormone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange electromyography and muscle biopsy to characterise the proximal myopathy
options.rationale: An inflammatory myopathy would be expected to raise the creatine kinase, which is normal, and invasive testing is not justified when the biochemistry already explains the weakness. These investigations belong where the metabolic screen is normal and creatine kinase is elevated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Commence high dose colecalciferol with calcium and review the response in three months
options.rationale: Severe vitamin D deficiency with a low calcium and phosphate, a raised alkaline phosphatase and secondary elevation of parathyroid hormone is the biochemical signature of defective bone mineralisation, and replacement with adequate dietary or supplemental calcium reverses it. Symptoms improve over weeks to months and the alkaline phosphatase is used to track healing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Osteomalacia is defective mineralisation of bone matrix in adults, most commonly from prolonged severe vitamin D deficiency, and it presents insidiously with proximal myopathy, diffuse bone pain and tenderness, waddling gait and fragility fractures. The biochemical pattern is characteristic and is what separates it from the conditions it mimics: low or low-normal calcium and phosphate, a raised alkaline phosphatase of bone origin, a markedly low 25-hydroxyvitamin D and a secondarily raised parathyroid hormone. In Australia the highest risk groups are people with darker skin, those who cover their skin for cultural or religious reasons, housebound and residential care residents, and people with malabsorption or on enzyme inducing medicines. Treatment is replacement with colecalciferol at loading doses followed by maintenance, together with ensuring adequate calcium intake, and clinical improvement precedes normalisation of the alkaline phosphatase. Antiresorptive drugs must not be started before repletion because of the risk of provoking hypocalcaemia.
key_points: Low calcium and phosphate with a high alkaline phosphatase and high parathyroid hormone is the signature
A raised parathyroid hormone with a low calcium indicates a secondary, appropriate response
Normal creatine kinase and inflammatory markers argue against myositis and polymyalgia rheumatica
Skin covering, darker skin, housebound status and malabsorption are the main Australian risk groups
Do not start a bisphosphonate before vitamin D and calcium are replete
explanation.pearls: Track healing with the alkaline phosphatase rather than the vitamin D level: it often rises transiently as mineralisation resumes before falling to normal over three to six months of adequate replacement.

subtopic_detail: Acute symmetrical polyarthritis after mosquito exposure
stem:
A 41 year old woman presents to your clinic with three weeks of pain and swelling in both wrists, both knees and the small joints of her hands, with two hours of morning stiffness. She has also had marked fatigue and a fine rash over her trunk that has now faded. She camped along the Murray River six weeks ago and recalls many mosquito bites.

On examination there is synovitis of both wrists and several metacarpophalangeal joints, with symmetrical distribution. There are no nail changes, no scaly plaques and no oral or genital ulcers. Rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies are negative, and hand radiographs show no erosions.

data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 28 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 44 mm/h (less than 20), full blood count within normal limits, antinuclear antibody negative, uric acid within normal limits

lead_in: Which investigation is most likely to establish the diagnosis?

options.text: Ross River virus and Barmah Forest virus IgM and IgG serology
options.rationale: An abrupt symmetrical polyarthritis with a transient rash and profound fatigue, three to six weeks after heavy mosquito exposure near an inland river system, fits epidemic polyarthritis, and paired alphavirus serology is the diagnostic test. Seronegative status and absent erosions support a post-infectious rather than an erosive process. (Source: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Ross River Virus Infection)
source_refs: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Ross River Virus Infection

options.text: Repeat anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody testing in six weeks
options.rationale: Seronegative rheumatoid arthritis is possible but repeating this antibody adds little when the tempo is acute and a clear arboviral exposure precedes the illness, and it would not explain the transient rash. Repeat testing is more useful when synovitis persists beyond three months without an alternative explanation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Human leucocyte antigen B27 typing and sacroiliac joint imaging
options.rationale: This pathway investigates spondyloarthritis, which presents with inflammatory back pain, asymmetrical large joint involvement or enthesitis rather than a symmetrical small joint pattern, and the absent psoriasis and ulcers remove the usual triggers. It would be indicated if she had buttock pain with alternating radiation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Extractable nuclear antigen panel and complement C3 and C4 levels
options.rationale: This connective tissue screen is driven by a positive antinuclear antibody, which is negative here, so the pre-test probability of a positive extractable nuclear antigen result is very low. The panel earns its place when there is cytopenia, proteinuria or a photosensitive rash. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Ultrasound guided aspiration of the right knee for crystals and culture
options.rationale: Aspiration is the priority in a hot single joint where septic arthritis or crystal disease is possible, but a three week symmetrical polyarthritis with normal uric acid is not that presentation. Synovial fluid analysis here would show non-specific inflammation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Ross River virus is the most commonly notified mosquito borne disease in Australia, with the classic syndrome of epidemic polyarthritis comprising acute symmetrical polyarthralgia or arthritis, fatigue and a transient maculopapular rash. The incubation period is usually three to 21 days and the illness often begins weeks after the exposure that a patient remembers. Diagnosis rests on serology, with IgM plus IgG or a fourfold rise in IgG on paired samples, noting that IgM alone can persist for months and is not sufficient in isolation. Management is symptomatic with simple analgesia, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and graded exercise, since no antiviral therapy exists. Most patients improve within three to six months, and the practical importance of making the diagnosis is to avoid committing a patient to disease modifying antirheumatic drugs for a self limiting illness.
key_points: Epidemic polyarthritis mimics early seronegative rheumatoid arthritis but follows an arboviral exposure
Symmetrical small joint synovitis with a transient rash and severe fatigue is the typical triad
Diagnosis requires alphavirus serology; isolated IgM can persist and is not sufficient alone
Absence of erosions and negative anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies argue against rheumatoid arthritis
Treatment is symptomatic, with most patients recovering over three to six months
explanation.pearls: Isolated Ross River virus IgM can persist for over 12 months and cannot confirm acute infection on its own: seek IgM with IgG seroconversion, or a fourfold IgG rise between samples taken 10 to 14 days apart.

sources.label: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Ross River Virus Infection

subtopic_detail: Severity scoring and corticosteroid decision in acute alcohol related hepatitis
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar reviewing a 47 year old man admitted with three weeks of deepening jaundice and abdominal swelling. He drinks approximately 15 standard drinks daily and stopped four days ago. He is tender in the right upper quadrant with a smooth palpable liver edge and shifting dullness.

He was started on intravenous fluids and thiamine on admission. A liver ultrasound with Doppler shows a coarse echotexture, patent hepatic and portal veins and moderate ascites, with no biliary dilatation. Diagnostic paracentesis yields a neutrophil count of 90 x10^6/L. Blood cultures and a viral hepatitis screen are negative, and his paracetamol level is undetectable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 268 micromol/L (less than 20), prothrombin time 22 s (control 12 s), aspartate aminotransferase 186 U/L (less than 40), alanine aminotransferase 74 U/L (less than 40), albumin 26 g/L (35-50), creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110), white cell count 13.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone and monitor the response at day seven
options.rationale: His discriminant function is well above 32, marking severe disease with high short term mortality, and active infection, gastrointestinal bleeding and renal failure have all been excluded, so corticosteroids are indicated. Response is reassessed around day seven to decide whether to continue or stop. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol Related Liver Disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol Related Liver Disease

options.text: Commence intravenous ceftriaxone and reassess the ascites in 48 hours
options.rationale: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis requires an ascitic neutrophil count of at least 250 x10^6/L, and his count of 90 x10^6/L is below that threshold with negative blood cultures, so empirical treatment is not justified. The raised white cell count reflects the hepatitis itself rather than infection. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol Related Liver Disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol Related Liver Disease

options.text: Commence oral pentoxifylline as the preferred alternative to corticosteroids
options.rationale: Pentoxifylline has not shown a survival benefit in controlled trials and is no longer recommended in place of a corticosteroid when steroids are not contraindicated. It was historically chosen for patients with sepsis or renal impairment, neither of which applies here. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Alcohol-related Hepatitis)

options.text: Arrange transjugular liver biopsy before any specific therapy is started
options.rationale: Biopsy is reserved for genuine diagnostic uncertainty, and delaying treatment in severe disease worsens outcomes when the clinical and biochemical picture is already characteristic. It would be justified if the aminotransferase pattern or serology suggested a competing diagnosis. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Alcohol-related Hepatitis)

options.text: Refer for liver transplantation assessment after six months of abstinence
options.rationale: A fixed six month abstinence rule would leave severe disease untreated during the period of highest mortality, and modern Australian practice individualises transplant assessment rather than applying an arbitrary interval. Transplant discussion belongs after failure of medical therapy, not instead of it. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol Related Liver Disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol Related Liver Disease

explanation.summary: Acute alcohol related hepatitis presents with rapid onset jaundice on a background of sustained heavy drinking, and the aspartate to alanine aminotransferase ratio typically exceeds two with absolute values usually under 300 U/L. Severity scoring with the Maddrey discriminant function, calculated from the prothrombin time prolongation and the bilirubin, separates patients with a short term mortality high enough to justify corticosteroids from those who do not benefit. Before steroids are started, active infection, gastrointestinal bleeding and significant renal impairment must be excluded, since each converts the treatment into a net harm. The Lille score at day seven identifies non-responders in whom continuing prednisolone adds infection risk without benefit. Alcohol cessation support, nutritional repletion and thiamine remain the interventions that determine long term survival regardless of the steroid decision.
key_points: A discriminant function above 32 defines severe disease and is the threshold for considering corticosteroids
Exclude sepsis, gastrointestinal bleeding and renal failure before starting a corticosteroid
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis requires an ascitic neutrophil count of at least 250 x10^6/L
An aspartate to alanine aminotransferase ratio above two with values under 300 U/L is characteristic
The day seven Lille score identifies non-responders in whom steroids should be stopped
explanation.pearls: The two numbers that decide the corticosteroid question are a Maddrey discriminant function above 32 to start and a day seven Lille score above 0.45 to stop, the latter marking non-response where continuing prednisolone only adds infection risk.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol Related Liver Disease
